turn_text: that's an incredible story. And looking back at your career in the house, if there was something you knew now that you wish you could tell your past self when you got elected to Congress, what would it be?

If I could tell my past self when I got elected, you know, I think that this is something that a lot of women maybe, in my experiences and the friends that I have as members of Congress, we don't really take credit for a lot of the things that we do. I'll give you an example. Stop Act was enacted into law. That is, stop taxpayer obligation to perpetrators of sexual harassment. If you remember the, administrative committee was trying to work through this fund that was out there that members of Congress would use to make sexual allegations go away. And I thought that was a problem for two reasons. And on both sides, first, it wasn't it didn't allow members of Congress to take responsibility, personal responsibility for their personal decisions and behaviors. And I didn't want them to be able to just get away with whatever. And it also felt like, as a member of Congress, if you didn't do anything wrong, that you would want to have your day. It protected due process. So I wanted them to go in and be able to debate and talk about what happened and stick up for themselves. And I didn't want somebody to just be paid off, and I also didn't want for people to take advantage of a fund that was out there. So on so many ends, I thought that taxpayers having to pay for bad behaviors of members of Congress was wrong on so many levels. So I actually enacted that bill, the Stop Act, and I went on to the next. And a lot of people don't know that that was a bill that was out there. First of all, it shouldn't have been there. That fund shouldn't have been there to begin with. But to be able to get that through and stop people like Blake Ferrant Ball and some other people from being able to use those funds, that was a major accomplishment. But it was more about getting it done than it was about taking credit for it. And unfortunately, I would tell myself to, you know what, make that known. Take credit for some of these things because people need to know that you're actually doing something. And it's just inherently counterintuitive for me. If I see something that needs to be done, I just did it and moved on to the next thing. When my kid spills milk, I don't sit there and say, hey, by the way, I cleaned it up. Look how great it looks. It just felt like it was my responsibility and moved on to the next thing. So I would tell myself back then to take a moment, take accountability, but also take the credit for getting something done because it's important for people to know what you've actually accomplished.

Yeah, so actually, a lot of people told me not to go into the Congressional Black Caucus, that it was going to be really uncomfortable. And these are people who, the first time I went in, actually, President Barack Obama was the president for two years. And then President Trump got elected two years after that. I remember going in and it was really uncomfortable. There was one point where we had a meeting at the White House and I had to be invited. I don't know if they wanted to invite me, but I was part of the Congressional Black Caucus. So I had to be invited. And I went and there was a table that was just had names all over it. And they had President Barack Obama and then the Vice President Joe Biden. and people came in and sat down and I was looking for my name and I couldn't find it anywhere. And all of a sudden on a chair next to the bathroom in the back of the room was a name tag for me. And I was just, I don't know what got into me, but I was like, I don't think so. Everybody got in. They sat down. They took their seats. And I noticed that there was a seat open at the table. I grabbed my tag and I said, excuse me, can you scooch in for a second to the vice president? I was like, can you scooch in a little bit? And he looked at me and he moved in and I think that he was kind of surprised that I actually, I don't know why he was the word scooch. Can you scooch in a little bit? But then I took, I put my tag in and I said, I'm not going to be sitting at the bathroom. I'm going to be sitting at the table. I am a member of Congress and I've served a spot just like everybody else. And I sat down. I'm not sure if that helped me build relationships, but I think at that point they knew that I wasn't going to be one to walk all over. But from then I really formed a really good friendship with, first of all, Marsha Fudge from Ohio. She became my big sister. And I can tell you that I have a genuine love for her. She was my diva that no one would mess with. I mean, if somebody gave me a hard time, she would straighten it out. And she also protected me on the floor. If there was a vote, she looked at me, she's like, you don't need to vote for this. This is not something you need to, and then there were times where she's like, looks at me, and she's like, you need to change your vote on this. You need to support this. And I got to the point where I knew that when she was giving me advice, it was really for me. Cedric Richmond, I became really good friends with him. He explained to me why he was a Democrat and why I was a Republican. They asked over and over and over again, and they had a path that they're like, no, she's part of our caucus. We're not going to campaign against her and they saw me as one of them.
